analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal income tax on profits from selling long-held investments.
analysis.headline: The bill to end capital gains taxes died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. David Dreier's bill would have rewritten the tax code so that no one would ever pay federal income tax on long-term capital gains — the profit from selling a stock, business, or property held more than a year. Because the overwhelming majority of capital gains go to the wealthiest households, the bill would have been, in effect, a large tax cut concentrated at the top, paid for by higher deficits or by shifting the burden to everyone else. It was introduced on October 7, 1994, weeks before the end of the congressional session, sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment gains would pay zero federal tax on profits from selling assets they held over a year. Capital gains are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest Americans, so the benefit would flow overwhelmingly to high-income households and to investors and financial firms whose activity the untaxed gains would encourage. Federal revenue would fall, meaning other taxpayers, or federal programs and deficit levels, would absorb the difference.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors with large asset gains

how_it_helps.text: The bill would exclude 100 percent of long-term capital gain from gross income, so investors would owe no federal income tax on profits from selling property held over the long term [S2][S3].
The exclusion would apply to sales and exchanges after December 31, 1994 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government loses the revenue it now collects on capital gains — a tax that falls mostly on high-income households. Unless replaced, that loss would be made up through larger deficits, spending cuts, or higher taxes on other income, so ordinary taxpayers and users of federal programs would ultimately bear the cost.

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the tax on long-term gains removes nearly all federal taxation of a form of income that is concentrated at the top, shifting the overall tax burden toward wages and other ordinary income [S2][S3].
The Treasury would lose billions in annual revenue, increasing deficits or forcing offsetting cuts and tax increases elsewhere [S2][S3].
Because gains are realized only when assets are sold, a zero rate rewards holding and can encourage tax-driven transactions, without directly creating jobs or new investment on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward, near-total tax cut for the wealthiest households, whose investment gains are the vast majority of all capital gains. Whatever stimulus might come from untaxed investment profit comes at the price of losing the primary federal tax on wealth appreciation, leaving the burden on wages and deficits. As drafted — two pages, no revenue offsets, no phase-ins — it offered no benefit to households with little or no investment income.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the session and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. David Dreier introduced the bill on October 7, 1994, near the end of the 103rd Congress [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, where it stayed; there is no record of a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote [S5].
The bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the federal government kept the capital gains tax and other taxpayers were spared the shifted burden; the main winners from the outcome are ordinary taxpayers and the Treasury, while high-income investors lost the chance at a zero rate.

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 7, 1994, to exclude all long-term capital gains from taxable income

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, chaired by Dan Rostenkowski (D) at the time
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one besides the Republican sponsor signed on, so no party breakdown exists; the tax-writing committee, then controlled by Democrats, simply never acted.

industries.note: They hold the vast majority of long-term capital gains, so a 100 percent exclusion would function as a large, permanent tax cut for them, with the revenue loss resting on other taxpayers.
Untaxed gains would raise after-tax returns on selling and trading assets, benefiting brokers, funds, and financial firms that profit from investment activity.
The Treasury would forgo the revenue it now collects on capital gains, a burden that would fall back on deficits or on taxes applied to other income.
